stories.headline: US proposes 25% tariff on India, 17% if trade deal is signed
stories.dek: The Commerce Ministry says the US notice is under examination and that India has no structural excess capacity in any sector, while it stays committed to an early trade agreement.
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative proposed a 25% tariff on Indian goods, falling to 17% if India signs a bilateral trade agreement. India's Commerce Ministry rejected the excess-capacity finding and said concerns should be settled in the trade talks.
body: The United States on Wednesday proposed a 25% tariff on imports from India, to be capped at 17% if the two countries conclude a bilateral trade agreement, after a Section 301 investigation into manufacturing overcapacity.

India's Commerce Ministry responded the same day, saying it had taken note of the USTR's Notice of Determination and Request for Comments, which covers 14 economies including India. "The Notice is currently under examination," it said.

The ministry said India engaged constructively throughout the investigation and that the Department of Commerce had stated India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector. It said trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of the ongoing negotiations.

"Government of India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement," the ministry said, referring to the framework announced on February 2, 2026 and the joint statement of February 7, 2026.

Hindustan Times reported that the USTR's 189-page report builds its case around Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat and the Production Linked Incentive scheme. It concludes that India's policies on manufacturing capacity are unreasonable and burden US commerce. The report says India runs trade surpluses in pharmaceuticals, steel and ICT goods. It also flags labour laws, market access barriers and rising imports of inputs from China.

Under the proposal, the deal rate for India would be one percentage point below Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand at 18%, and three points below Vietnam and China at 20%, according to figures in PTI and Mathrubhumi reports. The EU, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland face 15%, inclusive of standard duties. The USTR made no determination on Mexico or Norway. Reports said it was not immediately clear whether the one-point gap meets India's demand for an edge over Asian rivals.
The proposed tariffs exempt generic medicines in dosage form, hundreds of drug ingredients used in pharmaceuticals, and patented drugs, Hindustan Times reported.

USTR Jamieson Greer told CNBC the rates are "not really additive" and will not generally stack on existing duties. "In effect, it'll look more like a top-up," he said. He added that he did not expect any to take effect for a couple of months.

The think tank GTRI said the dual-rate structure recreates the reciprocal-tariff regime under a new name and is meant to push partners into signing one-sided deals. Abhik Sengupta of the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society said India consumes most of what it produces and is not exporting a domestic glut.
Written comments are due by January 5, 2027, and public hearings begin on January 25.
keyFacts: The US proposed a 25% tariff on Indian goods, or 17% if a trade deal is signed.
The Section 301 probe covered 16 jurisdictions; tariff proposals target 14 of them.
Written comments are due by January 5, 2027; hearings start January 25.
India says it has no structural excess capacity in any sector.
Generic medicines, drug ingredients and patented drugs are exempt from the proposed tariffs.
stories.background: The USTR opened its Section 301 investigations after the US Supreme Court overturned tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. India and the US announced a framework for an interim deal in February, and talks on an interim bilateral trade agreement are continuing. Commerce minister Piyush Goyal rejected the overcapacity charge at the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee in October.
stories.whyItMatters: The gap between 25% and 17% depends on whether India concludes a trade agreement with Washington, and the proposal sets a comment and hearing process before any tariffs take effect.

stories.headline: Madurai Collector apologises to Supreme Court over unlit Thiruparankundram lamp
stories.dek: The court will hear a contempt petition and an enforcement plea this week, while Governor Rajendra Arlekar has sought a report from Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
stories.summary: Madurai Collector Nishant Krishna apologised to the Supreme Court for not lighting the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepathoon, blaming the temple board. A contempt petition has been filed, and the Governor has sought a report from the chief minister.
body: Madurai Collector Nishant Krishna apologised to the Supreme Court on Wednesday for the failure to light the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepathoon stone pillar on Thiruparankundram hill, as the court agreed to hear a plea for enforcement of its November 20 order.

"I sincerely apologise for the lamp not been lit at the Deepathoon," Krishna said in a status report. He said he took "all the steps" between November 21 and 24 to obtain the temple's authorisation for a team to light the lamp, but that the Board of Trustees resolved on November 24 to light it at the customary place. He said he learnt of that decision only after the lamp was lit at 8.30 pm.

The temple board said it unanimously resolved to light the lamp at the Deepa Mandapam, near the Uchipillaiyar temple, to protect age-old customs and Agama rules. Its statement was signed by chairperson V Shanmugasundaram.

A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi declined to start contempt proceedings on its own. It asked parties to file applications and said it would consider the enforcement plea on Thursday or Friday.

The Hindu Dharma Parishad, represented by K K Ramesh, filed a contempt petition against Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments commissioner T G Vinay, Collector Krishna and police commissioner S Rajendiran. It alleges wilful disobedience. Petitioners including Rama Ravikumar argued that the passing of the festival date on November 24 cannot be a ground to deny the relief.

The district administration said it completed all arrangements and that the temple did not authorise any team until the last moment. State minister CTR Nirmalkumar said the lamp was lit at the Deepa Mandapam, directly above the presiding deity.

The Governor sought the report under Article 167(b) of the Constitution, according to South First and The Times of India, which cited reports and highly placed sources. An official told the Times of India the Governor seeks a factual report and asks no questions.

Hindu Munnani state president Kadeswara C Subramaniam met the Governor and said he told him the government should be dismissed. BJP leaders and Hindu groups protested at the foothills, and several people, including BJP state chief Nainar Nagenthran, were detained and later released. Scroll reported that some demonstrators vandalised buses and public property.

The Supreme Court's November 20 order allowed the lighting as a one-time measure, with access limited to authorised persons. It said the arrangement creates no customary, religious or proprietary right and left the wider dispute open.
keyFacts: The Supreme Court's November 20 order allowed a one-time lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon.
The lamp was lit at the Deepa Mandapam on November 24, not at the Deepathoon.
The contempt petition names the HR&CE commissioner, the Madurai Collector and the police commissioner.
The Governor sought a report under Article 167(b), according to sources cited by media.
stories.background: For decades the Karthigai Deepam was lit at the Deepa Mandapam on the lower slopes. Hindu groups sought permission to light it at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar higher up, about 50 metres from the Sikandar Badusha dargah. Madras High Court judge GR Swaminathan ruled in December that the pillar was a lamp-holding structure, and a division bench upheld the order in January. The state government challenged it in the Supreme Court, which stayed the High Court's findings on the pillar's nature and land ownership.
stories.whyItMatters: The Supreme Court's decision on the contempt petition and enforcement plea could determine whether the three named officials face proceedings and whether the lamp is lit at the Deepathoon.

stories.headline: Houthis say they hit Saudi Ras Tanura refinery; coalition reports drones downed
stories.dek: Saudi-led coalition said air defences destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura but did not say the refinery was struck, while Houthi forces advance on Aden.
stories.summary: Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, causing fires, and Riyadh's financial district. The Saudi-led coalition said it downed four drones, while Houthi forces advanced to about 60 kilometres from Aden.
body: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom's largest, and Riyadh's financial district, according to Reuters.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the refinery attack caused fires and that the group struck the financial district in three phases.

The Saudi-led coalition said earlier on Wednesday that air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, in the Eastern Province. It did not say the refinery had been struck. The Saudi government communications office and state oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

NASA satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters showed thick black smoke around the refinery, covering an area of about 600 square kilometres. Ras Tanura has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and sits in a complex on the Gulf coast that is a major export terminal for Saudi crude.

In Riyadh, Saudi civil defence said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday when a tower in the financial district was hit. The tower is the capital's tallest and houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the building in less than a week; the first, on November 19, caused damage but no injuries.

On the ground, Houthi forces have advanced to within about 60 kilometres of Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government, a military official said on Tuesday, according to France 24. Government-aligned forces have set up a fortified line to defend the city.

France 24 reported that the advance followed the withdrawal of government-allied forces from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which let the Houthis consolidate control of territory around the waterway. The New York Times described the Houthis as on a winning streak in an asymmetrical war of attrition against Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies.

The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, have fired at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, Reuters reported. Earlier attacks temporarily disrupted some Aramco operations and led to cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh.
keyFacts: Ras Tanura is Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, with capacity of 550,000 barrels per day.
The coalition said it destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura on Wednesday.
Eleven people were wounded on Tuesday in a strike on a Riyadh tower housing the Public Investment Fund.
Houthi forces are about 60 kilometres from Aden, a military official said.
The civil war reignited in July as a spillover from the US-Iran war.
stories.background: Yemen's civil war had been frozen before it reignited in July in a spillover from the US-Iran war, according to Reuters. Since then the Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings, forcing Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel events including the AFC Asian Cup and the FII investment conference. The US-Iran war also raised the importance of Yanbu on the west coast over the Gulf-coast export complex that includes Ras Tanura.
stories.whyItMatters: Attacks on Saudi oil facilities and Riyadh affect energy exports, flights and business events in the kingdom, and fighting near Aden threatens the government's provisional capital.

stories.headline: Nasdaq 100 briefly enters bear market as Nvidia leads tech sell-off
stories.dek: Chipmakers fell hardest on Wednesday as investors questioned AI spending, while US inflation data and proposed tariffs on 14 trading partners added to the selling.
stories.summary: The Nasdaq 100 fell 20% from its October record close during Wednesday's session, the usual bear-market threshold, as AI-linked shares extended losses. Nvidia dropped 8.7% as the lift from Jensen Huang's return as chief executive faded.
body: The technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% from its record close in October on Wednesday, the threshold commonly used to define a bear market, as investors sold AI-linked shares for a second straight session, Mint reported, citing Bloomberg and Reuters.

The Nasdaq Composite fell nearly 5% during the session, according to Mint. The WSJ said the Nasdaq led US indexes lower but recovered from its lows of the day. At 11:30 a.m. ET, the S&P 500 was down 3.2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 2.20%. Mint said the Nasdaq and S&P 500 were on track for their worst November since the 2008 global financial crisis.
Chipmakers led the declines. Nvidia fell 8.7% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 7.3%, Mint said. Alphabet lost 5%, Amazon 5.4%, Microsoft 3% and Apple 1.7%.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, slipped another 2.1% after closing below its $83 IPO price for the first time on Tuesday. The stock had briefly reached $115 on its first day of trading last week.

Nvidia's shares had jumped after Huang was reinstated as chief executive following his resignation earlier this month. The Guardian reported that the reinstatement lifted the stock more than 30% and added more than $900bn to its market value, but that it lost almost 6% by Tuesday's close. The BBC said the boost eased further on Wednesday. It linked Huang's resignation to revelations about extramarital affairs.
The BBC noted that Nvidia is both a supplier to and financier of many firms involved in the AI rollout, so its volatility has had a wider effect.

Fresh economic data added to the pressure. Core personal consumption expenditures prices, the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation, rose 0.3% in October. The annual core rate accelerated to 3.3%, above the 3.2% economists expected, Mint said. Overall inflation was 3.8%. The report said the data reinforced expectations of a Fed rate hike next month.
Other data was mixed. GDP grew at an annualised 4.3% in the third quarter, the strongest in three years, but consumer spending stalled in October, Mint reported.

The US also proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including the European Union and China, to counter what it describes as structural excess industrial capacity. According to Reuters, China faces an additional 20% on top of roughly 25% duties imposed during Donald Trump's first term.
keyFacts: Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% from its October record close on Wednesday.
Nvidia fell 8.7%; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 7.3%.
Core PCE inflation rose to 3.3% annually in October; overall inflation was 3.8%.
US proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including the EU and China.
Anthropic shares closed below the $83 IPO price on Tuesday.
stories.background: US stocks reached multiple record highs this year. Fund managers have since reassessed AI exposure over whether debt-funded investment can generate sufficient returns, Mint reported. The sector has also faced worries about regulatory scrutiny after the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections.
stories.whyItMatters: Big technology companies have helped shield the US economy from global shocks, the BBC noted, so a sustained fall in their shares affects the broader market and investors' portfolios.

stories.headline: US proposes tariffs of up to 20% on 14 economies after capacity probe
stories.dek: The US Trade Representative's proposal covers China, the EU and Japan, and would take effect no earlier than January after public comment and a hearing.
stories.summary: The US Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed tariffs of up to 20% on 14 economies, including China, the EU and Japan, after an eight-month probe into excess industrial capacity. The EU and China rejected the overcapacity charge.
body: The United States on Wednesday proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on imports from 14 economies, including China, the European Union and Japan, following an investigation into what Washington calls excess industrial production.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties after an eight-month probe into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners. The US accuses the targeted economies of promoting excess output that lets cheaper goods undercut American manufacturers.
The duties must go through a public comment period and a hearing. DW reported they could take effect in January at the earliest.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC the proposed rates would largely match those set under existing trade agreements, though some could be "topped up" by a few percentage points. A senior US administration official said the duties would respect the 15% cap agreed with the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and the 19% cap agreed with Malaysia.

China would face an additional 20%, the joint-highest rate. That would come on top of duties of around 25% imposed during Trump's first term, bringing the combined rate on some Chinese goods to 45%, according to DW. About $30 billion of Chinese imports that Washington is considering for tariff reductions would be exempt.

Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam are also covered. Mexico and Norway are excluded for now. Greer said talks with Mexico were continuing because the investigation into its trade practices was still open.

The proposed duties would not be added to existing sector tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium. They would also not stack with the 10% to 12.5% tariffs imposed in July on 60 partners over alleged inadequate action on forced labour; where both apply, the higher rate would prevail.
In a separate announcement, the USTR proposed higher tariffs on Brazilian raw and refined sugar and a new 10% duty on aircraft, which would affect Brazil's Embraer.

The EU said it would examine the proposal but rejected its basis. "We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity," it said, adding that it expected Washington to honour last year's trade agreement.

China also rejected the allegation but did not threaten retaliation. "The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

The proposal follows a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week. Trump is due to host Xi at the G20 summit in Miami in December. The existing US-China trade truce is set to expire on January 10.
keyFacts: The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20% on 14 economies on Wednesday.
China would face an additional 20%, taking some goods to a combined 45%.
The duties rely on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
Mexico and Norway are excluded for now; talks with Mexico continue.
The US-China trade truce is set to expire on January 10.
stories.background: The measures rely on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows Washington to investigate and retaliate against unfair foreign trade practices. They are intended in part to replace revenue lost after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs in February, ruling he lacked the authority to impose them by declaring an economic emergency.
stories.whyItMatters: Businesses may pass added costs to consumers, DW reported, at a time when US inflation reached 3.7% in September. The proposal also arrives before the January 10 expiry of the US-China trade truce.

stories.headline: Colombian forces free all hostages held 17 hours in Cartagena supermarket
stories.dek: One gunman was killed and four people were arrested, according to reports, after President De la Espriella said an armoured-car robbery went wrong and the suspects took hostages.
stories.summary: Colombian security forces stormed a Cartagena supermarket and freed all the hostages held there by gunmen for 17 hours. One assailant was killed, and President De la Espriella described the raiders as criminals, not a terrorist group.
body: Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena on Tuesday and freed all the hostages held there by armed men for 17 hours, according to BBC News, Al Jazeera and Press Trust of India.

One gunman was killed in the operation, BBC News and France 24 reported. France 24 said no hostages were injured. The BBC reported that four people were arrested and that their identities had not been released.

The headline figure of 76 hostages comes from the BBC. France 24 reported that some 25 people were freed in the final assault, after earlier releases. The BBC said the gunmen freed 10 hostages, among them elderly women, earlier in the day, and still held around 20 when the assault began.

President De la Espriella flew to Cartagena to oversee the operation. He called it "an extraordinary joint operation" carried out "flawlessly". He said the gunmen had been offered the chance to surrender and refused.

He said the men had no political affiliations. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said. He said they took hostages after a plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car was foiled.

Local media, cited by the BBC, reported that the gunmen asked for safe passage out of the supermarket and demanded nearly $2m and armoured vehicles. A police helicopter hovered over the building, in a popular shopping centre, and special forces prepared to enter.

Johan Correa, a rescued hostage who worked at the supermarket, told local media that men dressed as police officers came in at the start of his shift and began robbing the store. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police," he said. He said he and others were locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied, for more than four hours.

Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio the attackers wore masks and carried guns and knives. He said they repeatedly told hostages the exits were rigged with explosives.

Local media reported that authorities feared some gunmen might try to pass themselves off as hostages. The mayor of Cartagena said the freed hostages were being checked by medical teams and reunited with their families. Police said they had to stop some relatives from breaching the security perimeter while people were still inside.
keyFacts: The siege at the Cartagena supermarket lasted 17 hours, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera.
The BBC reported 76 people were held hostage; all were rescued.
One gunman was killed and four people were arrested, according to the BBC.
President De la Espriella travelled to Cartagena to oversee the operation.
The gunmen reportedly demanded nearly $2m and armoured vehicles, according to local media cited by the BBC.
stories.background: According to President De la Espriella, the gunmen planned to rob an armoured car carrying cash. The plan failed, and they then took the supermarket's staff and customers hostage.

stories.headline: India says military commanders held talks with China in Arunachal sector
stories.dek: The external affairs ministry said the discussions covered border management and outstanding issues along the LAC, and followed reports of friction in Upper Subansiri.
stories.summary: The external affairs ministry said senior Indian and Chinese military commanders met recently in the eastern sector to discuss border management and outstanding issues along the LAC. It was the second round of such talks in the Arunachal Pradesh sector since September.
body: Senior Indian and Chinese military commanders met in the eastern sector this month to discuss border management and outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control, the external affairs ministry said on Wednesday.

"A meeting of the senior, highest military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently," ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing, responding to a question on the talks. He said the discussions focused on "improving border management, as also addressing outstanding issues along the LAC".

Jaiswal said such interactions were aimed at maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and preventing any escalation. He added that India and China regularly engage through diplomatic and military mechanisms.

According to Hindustan Times, Lt Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Indian Army's 3 Corps, which is based near Dimapur in Nagaland, led the Indian side in the second week of November. A counterpart headed the Chinese side. The newspaper said the talks were believed to have lasted more than a week.

They were the second round of talks in the Arunachal Pradesh sector since September, when Kalia and a Chinese commander held flag talks in two sessions on either side of the LAC. Hindustan Times reported that the latest round followed reports of aggressive posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC, especially in the Upper Subansiri region.

Tensions arose between the Indian Army and the People's Liberation Army at Taksing, a remote area of Upper Subansiri district, in July and August, the newspaper reported. India said at the time that the two sides had agreed to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to "avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation".

The commander-level talks followed the 24th round of Special Representatives' talks between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi in New Delhi on August 19. That round produced 10 points of consensus, including mechanisms for talks between military commanders in the eastern and middle sectors of the LAC. A similar mechanism already exists in the western sector, which includes Ladakh.

Asked separately about reports that Pakistan may have used Chinese satellites to monitor Indian troop movements during Operation Sindoor in 2025, Jaiswal said: "We have seen some media reports on this particular issue. We will continue to closely follow the developments which may have a bearing on our security interests and take appropriate measures."
keyFacts: The MEA confirmed the commanders' meeting at a briefing on Wednesday.
It was the second round of talks in the Arunachal sector since September.
Lt Gen Girish Kalia of 3 Corps led the Indian side, per Hindustan Times.
The Special Representatives' talks on August 19 produced 10 points of consensus.
stories.background: A military face-off in Ladakh in 2020 lasted more than four years and took bilateral ties to a six-decade low, according to Hindustan Times. The two sides reached an understanding in October 2024 on disengaging frontline forces at several friction points in the Ladakh sector and have since taken steps to rebuild ties.
stories.whyItMatters: The talks use a mechanism agreed in August for the eastern sector, where India and China have reported friction. India has said the state of the border will determine the overall course of the relationship.

stories.headline: Israeli strike kills Hamas security official, wife and two daughters in Gaza City
stories.dek: The Israeli military said it killed Mohammed Abu al-Ouf a day after a strike that killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.
stories.summary: An Israeli airstrike on an apartment in Gaza City on Wednesday killed Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, a senior Hamas security official, his wife and two daughters, medics and Hamas said. Israel's military called him a significant figure; Hamas called the killing a crime.
body: An Israeli airstrike on an apartment in Gaza City early on Wednesday killed Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, who headed Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, along with his wife and two daughters, Gaza's Hamas-run Interior Ministry and medics said.

The ministry named the dead as Abu al-Ouf, his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13. Medics said the strike hit the building in the Shati, or Beach, refugee camp in western Gaza City, near the coast. Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal, quoted by the South China Morning Post, said four people were killed and 12 wounded. The civil defence operates under Hamas. Al Jazeera reported that six others died alongside him; the sources do not reconcile the figures.

The Israeli military confirmed it had killed Abu al-Ouf. It described him as a significant figure who had served as "a key source of expertise in efforts to restrict the IDF's counterterrorism operations in the Gaza Strip". It said he had helped advance attacks on Israeli forces and civilians, during the war and more recently, and had worked to restore Hamas's capabilities in violation of the ceasefire.
In a separate statement, the military said he belonged to a Hamas cell that held Israeli officer Oron Shaul captive in Gaza for years. Hamas did not immediately comment on that claim.
The interior ministry condemned the strike as a "heinous crime". It accused Israel of targeting security personnel "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".

The strike followed one on Tuesday in western Gaza City that killed Naeem Abu Nahel, head of Hamas's internal security service for all of Gaza. The Israeli military said Abu al-Ouf's killing followed "yesterday's elimination of his commander". Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said after Tuesday's strike there was no escape for Hamas from Israel's "long reach".
Medics said another Israeli strike later on Wednesday hit the Karama neighbourhood in northern Gaza City and killed one person.

The BBC reported that Abu al-Ouf's service enforces discipline, protects Hamas infrastructure and roots out informants. Abu Nahel had held his post only since September, when his predecessor was captured by Israeli special forces in Gaza City.
keyFacts: Mohammed Abu al-Ouf headed Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza.
His wife Noura, 41, and daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13, were also killed, the interior ministry said.
Naeem Abu Nahel, Hamas's internal security chief for Gaza, was killed in a strike on Tuesday.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza since the October ceasefire, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.
stories.background: A ceasefire took effect in Gaza in October 2025, but near-daily Israeli strikes have continued. stories.headline: MEA says Saurav Das told not to use passport over birthplace discrepancy
stories.dek: The Delhi High Court is due to hear on Thursday the CJP co-convener's challenge to being stopped at the airport, after the ministry cited inputs from law enforcement authorities.
stories.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs said the Chennai passport office served Cockroach Janta Party co-convener Saurav Das a show-cause notice over his place of birth and advised him not to use his passport. Das says the notice was meant to stop his UK trip; the Delhi High Court hears his plea on Thursday.
body: The Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday that the Regional Passport Office (RPO) in Chennai had served Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Saurav Das a show-cause notice over discrepancies in his place of birth, and had advised him not to use his passport until he replies.

Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a media briefing that the notice was issued on November 23 and gave Das seven days to respond. He said it followed reports from "relevant law enforcement authorities". He did not name the authorities.

"If, at any stage, a discrepancy is noted or reported by the authorities, amounting to a suppression of facts, we issue a show-cause notice to the applicant, allowing them to present their side of the matter," Jaiswal said. He described the step as established procedure.

Das was stopped at the immigration counter at Indira Gandhi International Airport on the night of November 23. He was due to fly to London at 1 am on Tuesday for talks on what he calls the "cockroach movement". He named Oxford, Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Edinburgh as hosts.

Das said he received the notice about five hours before his flight. The Wire reported that it was emailed to him at 7.30 pm on Monday. He called it a "cowardly ploy" to curb his freedom of speech. He said his passport was issued in 2019 and that he had travelled abroad on it before. NDTV reported that the passport was issued on August 21, 2019 and reportedly lists Chennai as his birthplace.

Das also said no order or Look Out Circular was shown to him at the airport. His counsel told the Delhi High Court: "I was stopped at immigration. No order was shown to me. [There is] no LOC (lookout circular) or prohibition by any authority from letting me travel."

The matter was mentioned before Acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma on Wednesday. Counsel said Das could still reach the UK on November 27, with a flight on Thursday. The bench listed the plea for Thursday. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal is to argue it, according to Hindustan Times.

Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor accused Das of making misleading claims. He said the event was organised by the Oxford Union, a student debating society independent of the university. He also alleged that Das wanted to go abroad "to defame India from abroad on Constitution Day, November 26". Das has not been quoted in the sources responding to this.
keyFacts: The Chennai RPO issued the show-cause notice to Saurav Das on November 23, seeking a reply within seven days.
Das was advised not to use his passport until he submits his response.
Das says his passport was issued on August 21, 2019.
The Delhi High Court is due to hear his plea on Thursday, November 26.
stories.background: Das, a journalist known for his work on the judiciary and who lives in Delhi, is co-convener of the Cockroach Janta Party. He said he was travelling to speak on the "cockroach movement" at UK universities. NDTV described the planned event as one on recent protests against the Narendra Modi government.
stories.whyItMatters: The court's decision will determine whether Das can travel to the UK on his planned November 27 arrangements, and it will test the basis on which a passport holder can be stopped at immigration.

stories.headline: Congress's Imran Masood says 'we aren't begging' after SP offers 26 seats for UP polls
stories.dek: The Samajwadi Party named candidates for five seats during talks, and Akhilesh Yadav asked Congress to identify more winnable seats beyond the 26 offered.
stories.summary: Congress MP Imran Masood said his party would decide whether to continue seat-sharing talks with the Samajwadi Party, which offered 26 seats and named five candidates. Akhilesh Yadav said both parties should look for an 'equation for victory'.
body: Congress Uttar Pradesh working committee chief Imran Masood said on Wednesday that his party would decide whether to continue seat-sharing talks with the Samajwadi Party (SP), after the SP named candidates for five assembly seats while negotiations were under way, PTI reported.

"We aren't begging," Masood told PTI. "The deal has to be mutually acceptable, respectable." He said: "When you are holding talks on one hand and making announcements on the other, it shows that you are not serious."
Speaking to NDTV, Masood repeated the "beggar" remark. "We are not beggars that you will give us whatever you want," he said, adding: "We don't need instructions from Akhilesh ji."

The first round of talks ended inconclusively on Tuesday at Congress leader Pramod Tiwari's Delhi residence. SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav said his party had offered Congress 26 of the 403 assembly seats. NDTV reported, citing an understanding within Congress, that the party first sought 181 seats, then cut its list to 131 and then 110. Scroll, citing India Today, reported that Congress submitted a revised list of about 100 to 120 seats on Monday.

Of the five SP candidates, four are sitting MLAs: Ashu Malik in Saharanpur, Nahid Hasan in Kairana, Umar Ali Khan in Behat and Mehboob Ali in Amroha. The fifth, Jyoti Lodhi, will contest from Lalitpur. Saharanpur falls in Masood's Lok Sabha constituency. NDTV, citing sources, said Behat and Saharanpur are also on Congress's wishlist.

On Tuesday, Akhilesh Yadav asked Congress to name more constituencies beyond the 26. "Based on our assessment and the mathematical equation for victory, we may also be able to tell the Congress about many winnable seats it has not even considered for some reason," he said. He added: "This is not about seats, but about victory."

Masood questioned that approach. "If they have the guarantee of winnability, then why didn't they make a government in 2022?" he asked. He also objected to the list of 26 seats being communicated through the media.

SP leaders offered differing responses. Shivpal Yadav said: "The alliance will remain; everything will be sorted out." Udai Veer Singh said the party had named candidates only on seats SP held in 2022, and that it had followed the same practice of gradual announcements in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.

SP MP Iqra Hasan called Masood's remarks "irresponsible" and "derogatory", saying an alliance is bigger than any one individual's ego. SP MP Zia Ur Rahman Barq called it "for the time being, a personal matter".
NDTV reported that leaders of both parties indicated another round of talks would be held within days, and that two such sittings may be needed to settle the seat-sharing.
keyFacts: SP has offered Congress 26 of Uttar Pradesh's 403 assembly seats.
SP named candidates for Saharanpur, Kairana, Behat, Amroha and Lalitpur during the talks.
The first round of talks ended inconclusively on Tuesday at Pramod Tiwari's Delhi residence.
In 2024 Lok Sabha polls, SP gave Congress 17 of 80 seats; Congress won six.
stories.background: The two parties contested the 2022 state elections separately. The BJP won 255 seats, the SP 111 and Congress two. They revived their alliance for the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, in which the SP won 37 seats and Congress six. The state elections are expected early next year.
stories.whyItMatters: The outcome of the talks will determine how the two INDIA bloc parties contest Uttar Pradesh's 403 seats in the 2027 assembly elections.

stories.headline: Supreme Court says students who opted for three languages may continue with them
stories.dek: The court said orally that pupils need not switch back to two languages, while hearing a CBSE plea to modify its September 28 order on Class 6.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court said on Wednesday that students who have already opted for three languages this academic year may continue with that choice. The remark came during a hearing on a CBSE plea to modify the court's September 28 order.
body: The Supreme Court on Wednesday, November 25, orally observed that students who have already opted for three languages for the current academic year may continue with that option and need not switch back to two.

The observation came as the court heard a plea by the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE). The board sought modification of a September 28 order that extended to Class 6 students the relaxation already available to Class 7 under the three-language formula.

Under that relaxation, students in Classes 7, 8 and 9 were given a transitional exemption from the CBSE Board examination in the third language when they reach Class 10. The third language will be assessed only through internal, school-based evaluation and will not count towards final Board results.

Under CBSE guidelines, students in Classes 7 to 9 were exempted, while the present Class 6 batch had been slated for full implementation. That would include a mandatory Board examination in the third language in Class 10 by 2031.

In earlier hearings, before it passed the September 28 order, the court had proposed making the scheme mandatory for Class 6 only from January 1, 2027. It was against what it called "springing a surprise" on the current Class 6 batch with only a few months of the academic year left.
Chief Justice Kant had said the government could use the time to develop incentives for children to take up a third language in schools.
keyFacts: The remarks were made orally on Wednesday, November 25, 2026.
CBSE sought modification of the Supreme Court's September 28 order on Class 6.
Classes 7 to 9 are exempt from a Board exam in the third language.
The third language will be assessed only internally for the exempted classes.
The Class 6 batch had been slated for a mandatory Class 10 Board exam in the third language by 2031.
stories.background: CBSE guidelines exempted students in Classes 7 to 9 from the Board exam in a third language, while the present Class 6 batch was to face full implementation. On September 28, the Supreme Court extended the Class 7 relaxation to Class 6 students. It had earlier proposed making the scheme mandatory for Class 6 only from January 1, 2027.

stories.headline: Court sets aside panel report that exposed Ramaphosa to impeachment
stories.dek: The Western Cape High Court ruled the parliamentary panel's 2022 Phala Phala findings unlawful, though opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the decision.
stories.summary: South Africa's Western Cape High Court on Wednesday set aside in its entirety an independent panel's report that said President Cyril Ramaphosa had a case to answer over the Phala Phala theft. Opposition parties have indicated they will challenge the ruling.
body: The Western Cape High Court on Wednesday declared unlawful and set aside an independent parliamentary panel's report that had found President Cyril Ramaphosa may have a case to answer over the 2020 theft of cash from his Phala Phala farm.

Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana, reading a unanimous decision, said the panel had "misconstrued its function, the nature of the inquiry it was to conduct and the recommendation it was required to make". She said it went beyond its lawful remit and made several material errors of law. The report was "reviewed and set aside in its entirety".
The court also declared unlawful the steps parliament had taken in relation to the report.

The panel, appointed by parliament, reported in 2022 that Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct. It said there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen". Ramaphosa has denied wrongdoing.

He confirmed a robbery took place at the Limpopo game farm but has said the money came from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business. BBC News reported that the theft involved $580,000 hidden in a sofa. Several investigations have cleared him, and BBC reported that two people were found guilty of the theft earlier this month.

Ramaphosa first challenged the report in court but withdrew the application after parliament voted against adopting its findings. He revived the case in May, after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him and ordered it to refer the report to an impeachment committee. In his latest challenge he argued the panel had "misconceived its mandate".

BBC News said the ruling effectively removes the basis for the impeachment process, unless parliament or others successfully appeal. If an appeal succeeded, the committee could examine the charges and make a recommendation. Removal would need a two-thirds majority in parliament, and the BBC reported that Ramaphosa's African National Congress has enough seats to block it.

Legal expert Richard Calland told the BBC the process was "dead in the water" and that any party wanting to revive it "would have to come up with a whole new basis". He said opposition parties would likely appeal, but parliament was unlikely to do so.

Political analyst Khanyi Magubane said the ruling was not a criminal finding about the farm but a verdict on the panel's report. "He does get significant reprieve ... but there will always be the shadow of the Phala Phala report," she said.
keyFacts: The Western Cape High Court set aside the panel report "in its entirety" on Wednesday.
The panel reported in 2022 that Ramaphosa may have a case to answer.
The theft at Phala Phala took place in 2020; BBC reported $580,000 was stolen.
Impeachment would need a two-thirds majority in parliament, according to BBC News.
Opposition parties have indicated they intend to challenge the ruling.
stories.background: The matter became known as "Farmgate" after former spy chief Arthur Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, reported it to police in 2022. He accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from police and tax authorities. Ramaphosa is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under rules introduced in 2018, according to the BBC.
stories.whyItMatters: The ruling removes the report on which the current impeachment process rested, unless an appeal succeeds. Parliament's committee would then be unable to examine the charges against the president.

stories.headline: Rupee hits eight-month high, wipes out FY27 losses as Sensex gains 1.8%
stories.dek: Foreign fund inflows and Brent crude slipping below $90 a barrel supported both the currency and equities, analysts said, though some expect consolidation.
stories.summary: The rupee climbed to an eight-month high against the dollar on Wednesday, recovering its losses for FY27, while the Sensex and Nifty rose about 1.8%. Analysts credited foreign inflows and Brent crude below $90 a barrel.
body: The rupee rose to an eight-month high against the dollar on Wednesday, erasing its losses for the 2026-27 fiscal year, as foreign inflows and Brent crude below $90 a barrel lifted the Sensex 1.82%.

In early interbank trade the rupee opened at 92.65 and touched 92.29, up 56 paise from its previous close of 92.85 on Monday, according to The Hindu. That level compared with the 92.28 close recorded on March 16. Later in the day the rupee was quoted at 92.23, up 62 paise, after touching 92.1850 during intraday trade.

Currency markets were shut on Tuesday for Prakash Gurpurb. The rupee has gained over 1.6% in five sessions since closing at 94.19 on November 13, and has recovered nearly 5% from its lowest-ever level of 96.88 on October 8.

Kunal Sodhani, head of treasury at Shinhan Bank, attributed the rise to strong foreign portfolio investor inflows, softer crude and better domestic dollar supply. He said November inflows into Indian equities stood at $14 billion so far. He also cited Reserve Bank of India measures that had curbed speculative positions, and more dollar selling by exporters.

The 30-share Sensex gained 1,502 points to close at 83,938. The 50-share Nifty rose 470 points, or 1.85%, to 25,819. The Sensex had risen as much as 2,062.22 points to 84,498.21 during the session. Investors' wealth increased by ₹3.49 lakh crore to ₹5,12,48,042.08 crore.

HUL rose 5.94%, Trent 3.59%, ICICI Bank 3.44%, Indigo 3.24%, HDFC Bank 3.18% and Bajaj Finance 3.04%. FMCG, pharma, financial services, banking and auto were the main sectoral gainers, while metal and media lagged. The Nifty Midcap 100 gained 0.30% and the Nifty Smallcap 100 fell 0.44%.

Shrikant Chouhan of Kotak Neo said he expected the Nifty to consolidate broadly in a 25,000–26,000 range in the very short term. Pabitro Mukherjee of Bajaj Broking said selling pressure at higher levels showed profit booking near key resistance zones.

Sodhani said the rupee could test 92.00 to 91.50 if conditions hold, but RBI dollar purchases could limit gains. He named a reversal in FPI flows, higher crude or renewed dollar strength as triggers for a correction.
keyFacts: The rupee reached 92.29 per dollar on Wednesday, against a 92.28 close on March 16.
The Sensex closed up 1,502 points, or 1.82%, at 83,938; the Nifty rose 1.85% to 25,819.
Brent crude traded 1.58% lower at $89.96 a barrel in futures during the day.
November foreign inflows into Indian equities stood at $14 billion so far, according to Shinhan Bank.
FIIs bought equities worth ₹5,672.99 crore on a net basis on Monday, exchange data showed.
stories.background: The rupee touched a lifetime low of 96.88 against the dollar on October 8. It closed at 94.19 on November 13 and at 92.85 on Monday, when the benchmark indices ended nearly 2% lower. Foreign institutional investors were net buyers that day.
stories.whyItMatters: A stronger rupee and cheaper crude lower import costs, and analysts said this could ease inflation expectations and help fuel-consuming sectors such as aviation, auto and paints.

stories.headline: Net FDI into India falls to lowest in over 5.5 years in September
stories.dek: Outflows exceeded inflows by nearly $5 billion as gross inflows slumped and repatriation of profits hit a high, though April-September net FDI remained above last year's level.
stories.summary: Net foreign direct investment into India was negative $4.95 billion in September 2026, the lowest since at least March 2021, according to RBI data. Gross inflows fell while outflows rose about 40% from August.
body: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India fell to negative $4.95 billion in September 2026, its lowest level since at least March 2021, as outflows exceeded inflows by nearly $5 billion, according to Reserve Bank of India data reported by The Hindu.
March 2021 is the earliest month for which the data are available. The Hindu said the fall came from a slump in gross inflows combined with a jump in outflows.
Gross inflows, the total direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September. That was 46.6% lower than in August and 17.6% lower than in September 2025.
The RBI said about two-thirds of gross inflows went into manufacturing, communication and computer services. Singapore and the United States were the main source countries.

Total outflows rose to $10.8 billion, nearly 40% higher than in August and 15% higher than in September last year. Repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India reached $6.4 billion. That is nearly 37% above the same month last year and the highest since at least March 2021.

Outward investment by Indian companies rose to $4.4 billion, a five-month high. According to the RBI, manufacturing and financial, insurance and business services accounted for about four-fifths of it. The Netherlands, Singapore and the US were the main destinations.
Despite September's figure, net FDI in the first half of the financial year, April to September 2026, was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year, The Hindu reported.

The RBI's November Bulletin, released on Wednesday, said the Indian economy stood out while global performance was uneven. It said net inflows under external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong, and that foreign portfolio inflows supported equity markets.
keyFacts: Net FDI in September 2026 was -$4.95 billion, lowest since at least March 2021.
Gross inflows fell to $5.9 billion, down 17.6% from September 2025.
Total outflows rose to $10.8 billion, about 40% above August.
Profit repatriation by foreign firms reached $6.4 billion, a high since at least March 2021.
April-September net FDI was more than 20% above the year-earlier period.
stories.background: Direct investment gives the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production. Portfolio investment is typically a minor shareholding. Net FDI is gross inflows minus outflows, which include profit repatriation and outward investment by Indian companies.

stories.headline: Petition creator says cyber police asked her to remove Sheshnag lake appeal
stories.dek: J-K Congress president Tariq Hameed Karra separately demanded a white paper on the project and questioned why the National Green Tribunal has not acted.
stories.summary: Businesswoman Zarqua Banday said on Wednesday that Cyber Police asked her to take down her online petition against construction near Sheshnag lake. The petition has over 11,000 verified signatures, and parties are trading charges over the work.
body: Zarqua Banday, a Kashmir-based entrepreneur who started an online petition against construction near Sheshnag lake on the Amarnath Yatra route, said on Wednesday that Cyber Police asked her to take it down.

"So, I received a call from the Cyber Police, asking me to take the petition down because it's illegal," Banday wrote in a post on her LinkedIn profile. She said she needed to consult people in her network who come from law and advocacy. The reports did not carry any response from the police.

The Change.org petition, titled "Stop construction around Kashmir's Alpine lakes", has more than 11,000 verified signatures. It seeks a halt to activity near the lake in Anantnag district and asks authorities to work with local environmental and community groups. It proposes guided trekking, limited access permits and eco-friendly accommodation instead of roads.
The Border Roads Organisation said on Monday that post-Yatra works are being carried out in compliance with all applicable safety norms and environmental safeguards.
Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, Kashmir's chief cleric, said he had signed the petition. In a post on X he asked why Chief Minister Omar Abdullah was silent.

PDP president Mehbooba Mufti and two party MLAs set out towards Sheshnag from Chandanwari on Tuesday but were stopped by police. She said machines and bulldozers were excavating a few kilometres from the Amarnath cave and warned of harm to the environment and the pilgrimage.

In Jammu on Wednesday, J&K Congress president Tariq Hameed Karra asked the government to issue a white paper naming the project, the agencies involved and the authorities that issued no objection certificates. He said the National Green Tribunal's failure to take cognisance of the alleged violations raised serious questions about its functioning. He recalled that an earlier road attempt between 2003 and 2008 was halted after the Supreme Court intervened.

The J&K BJP, through spokesperson Girdhari Lal Raina, said on Tuesday that the issue was being used to manufacture controversy and exploit religious sentiments. Vishva Hindu Parishad's J&K-Ladakh president Rajesh Gupta backed the BRO's track-widening and safety works, saying pilgrim safety must remain paramount.
Gupta demanded that the area along the Pahalgam and Baltal routes be declared the 'Shri Amarnathji Yatra Teerth Kshetra' and placed under the Shri Amarnathji Shrine Board.
keyFacts: Zarqua Banday's Change.org petition has more than 11,000 verified signatures.
Banday said Cyber Police called her and called the petition illegal.
Tariq Hameed Karra demanded a white paper on Wednesday.
The BRO said on Monday that works follow safety and environmental norms.

stories.background: Sheshnag lake lies in Anantnag district on the Pahalgam route to the Amarnath cave. A video of an excavator near the lake drew objections from political parties, religious leaders and environmentalists. The BRO is carrying out track-widening and safety works along the route.

stories.headline: Trump's investment accounts traded Nvidia shares at least 44 times this year, records show
stories.dek: The disclosures cover January to September, before Jensen Huang resigned and was reinstated as CEO, and Republican senators have joined Democrats in questioning the White House's role.
stories.summary: Donald Trump's portfolios bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 44 times this year, according to a BBC review of his financial disclosures. The White House says third parties manage the accounts, while senators from both parties question his role in Jensen Huang's return.
body: Donald Trump's investment portfolios bought or sold shares in the chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, according to a BBC Verify review of the US president's financial disclosures published on Wednesday.

The most recent disclosures, filed with the Office of Government Ethics, show that between January and September the portfolios bought between $5.2m and $17m of Nvidia stock and sold between $4.4m and $12m. They held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025. The filings report ranges rather than exact values, so a more precise analysis is not possible.

The disclosures do not cover the recent turmoil at Nvidia. Huang, the company's co-founder and chief executive, resigned on November 12 after reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman who has been alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price fell sharply.

On Monday, Nvidia's board announced that the 63-year-old Huang was being reinstated. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk". Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the board. Nvidia's shares rose 31% that day, adding about $1tn to its market value, though they remain below their level before the reports about Huang emerged.

The Financial Times calculated that the rally could have added as much as $15 million to Trump's holdings on Monday. It estimated he may have owned as many as 370,000 Nvidia shares on September 30, assuming purchases at the top of each disclosed range and sales at the bottom. The estimate is an upper bound, not a reported figure.

The White House has said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and that neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator for Arizona, said: "We need to investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement." Several Republican senators have also criticised the administration's role, according to the Daily Wire. John Curtis of Utah asked who in government had advised the board and on what basis. Rick Scott of Florida said the episode "looks terrible on its face".

Tom Cotton of Arkansas, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, said Congress had "much to investigate" and promised to pass chip export-control bills. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota cited the risk of extortion of Huang. Trump told CNBC he did not believe the woman involved was a Chinese spy.

The BBC said its analysis does not include other investment products Trump holds that may contain Nvidia shares. Nvidia's board is conducting an independent investigation into reports that foreign intelligence targeted Huang.
keyFacts: Trump's portfolios traded Nvidia shares at least 44 times this year, per the BBC's review of disclosures.

stories.headline: Bangladesh deploys 108 border guard platoons in seven districts before Hasina's planned return
stories.dek: Border Guard Bangladesh said 56 of the platoons are in Gopalganj, Sheikh Hasina's home district, where police have reported arson and vandalism in recent days.
stories.summary: Border Guard Bangladesh announced on Wednesday it had deployed 108 platoons across seven districts on the Home Ministry's instructions. Sheikh Hasina, in exile in India since August 2024, plans to return on December 16, her spokesperson said.
body: Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said on Wednesday it had deployed 108 platoons in seven districts, on the instructions of the Home Ministry, as the government braced for the planned return of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina from exile in India.

In a press statement, the BGB said the deployment was "to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and deal with any untoward situation", bdnews24.com reported. Of the total, 56 platoons are in Gopalganj, a stronghold of Hasina's Awami League. The others are 18 in Dhaka, 18 in Gazipur, six in Narayanganj, three in Chattogram, two in Mymensingh and one in Cox's Bazar. Four more platoons are on alert. One platoon has 30 to 40 personnel.

Police data cited by local media said 83 vehicles were set on fire and crude bombs were hurled at 87 locations between November 7 and 19. Police blamed activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations for several incidents. The party's activities are banned.

Gopalganj saw attacks and arson at two police stations and at the homes of two lawmakers of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) during the Awami League's November 19 lockdown call. The programme did not draw significant mobilisation on the ground, The Hindu reported. Last week about 2,000 police personnel, 10 BGB platoons and Special Response Battalion personnel were sent to the district.

Prothom Alo, citing police, reported that intelligence inputs pointed to possible covert attacks and sabotage. Leaders of the BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party were reportedly alerted as potential targets. Police also warned that weapons and explosives could be smuggled across the border.

Law enforcement in the 30 districts that border India has been told to step up surveillance, patrols and searches. Police spokesperson Kamarum Munira said police were on maximum alert to prevent sabotage, illegal infiltration and disruption of law and order.
The Awami League is promoting a lockdown programme for November 29 and 30 through online platforms.

Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said on Tuesday she plans to return on December 16, Victory Day, and has asked Dhaka to arrange her air travel from New Delhi on the national carrier. The Bangladesh government responded that she would be brought back "in handcuffs" and treated like any other convicted fugitive abroad.

Hasina, 79, has been sentenced to death in absentia by a special tribunal over the 2024 crackdown on protesters. She has denied wrongdoing and questioned the proceedings. Bangladesh has sought her extradition; India has acknowledged the requests but announced no decision.

stories.background: Hasina fled Dhaka in August 2024 after a student-led uprising toppled her government and has stayed in India since. She ruled for 15 years. Bangladesh has 64 districts, 30 of which border India.
stories.whyItMatters: The deployment affects security in Dhaka, Gazipur, Gopalganj and other districts, and sets the backdrop for the November 29 and 30 lockdown call and Hasina's announced December 16 return date.

stories.headline: Uddhav faction tells Supreme Court dissent claim can be used to topple governments
stories.dek: Senior advocate Kapil Sibal argued that the Maharashtra assembly speaker erred by treating the Shinde group's legislative majority as proof it was the original Shiv Sena.
stories.summary: The Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena faction told the Supreme Court on Wednesday that permitting a shift in allegiance under the guise of dissent could let elected governments be destabilised. It challenged the Shinde group's claim of legitimate dissent in the party split case.
body: The Uddhav Thackeray-led faction of the Shiv Sena told the Supreme Court on Wednesday that allowing legislators to shift political allegiance under the guise of dissent could make elected governments vulnerable to engineered defections.

Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for the faction, argued before a bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. He said that if such shifts were permitted, governments could be destabilised by engineering defections even among a handful of legislators.

Sibal also told the court that the Maharashtra assembly speaker committed a constitutional error. According to Mid-Day, he argued that the speaker treated the legislative majority of the Eknath Shinde group as proof that it represented the original Shiv Sena.

The submissions challenge the Shinde group's position that its actions amounted to legitimate dissent within the party. The sources available did not detail the Shinde group's response at Wednesday's hearing.

The Press Trust of India reported the argument under the headline that shifting political allegiance under the guise of dissent can topple elected governments. Its full report was not available for this account.

stories.headline: Meta executives meet Congress leaders over bias allegations in content moderation
stories.dek: Neither side has commented officially on the Tuesday meeting, which followed Indian Youth Congress protests outside Meta offices and the blocking of two party Instagram accounts.
stories.summary: Meta executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog met Congress leaders including Supriya Shrinate in Delhi on Tuesday, sources said. The party alleges its content is restricted while similar BJP posts stay up; Meta said it treats all parties neutrally.
body: Meta executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog met Congress leaders, including social media department head Supriya Shrinate, in Delhi on Tuesday, November 24, to discuss the party's allegations of bias in the platform's content moderation, according to sources.

Neither Meta nor the Congress has made an official comment on the meeting. Congress sources told The Hindu it took place at Meta's request. The South China Morning Post, citing four people familiar with the matter, reported that it was held behind closed doors at Congress headquarters and that the two sides were trying to defuse the protests.

The Indian Youth Congress (IYC) has held demonstrations outside Meta offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram. It alleges that political content posted by Congress leaders is being restricted while similar content from BJP leaders remains accessible. The Hindu also published a photo of a billboard in Bengaluru, put up by Karnataka's Youth Congress, carrying an altered image of Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

According to sources cited by The Hindu, Meta told the Congress delegation that its moderation policy and takedowns mostly concerned AI-generated content. Ms Shrinate is said to have replied that AI-generated BJP content targeting Congress leaders was not being removed.

She is also said to have argued that the youth wing's protests began after the official Instagram handles of IYC chief Uday Bhanu Chhib and of Manish Sharma, the All India Congress Committee in-charge for the IYC, were blocked. IYC sources said both handles have since been restored.

People familiar with the discussions said Meta restated its moderation policies and explained how restrictions are applied across its platforms, particularly for synthetically generated content. The company maintained that it takes a neutral approach to all political parties and made no commitments on the Congress's demands, the sources said.

stories.headline: US core inflation gauge rises to 3.8%; MCX gold falls ₹4,423 on Fed hike bets
stories.dek: The Fed's preferred inflation measure rose to its highest since May, strengthening expectations of a December rate increase and lifting the dollar.
stories.summary: The US personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, the highest since May. MCX gold futures fell 3.6% to ₹1,17,906 per 10 grams and silver dropped ₹8,800 to ₹1,36,712 per kg.
body: The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the US Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, showed annual inflation of 3.8% in October, the highest since May, and gold and silver prices fell sharply on the MCX on Wednesday.

The 3.8% figure is on a seasonally adjusted basis. CNBC reported that it matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast. The Guardian said prices rose as energy prices climbed sharply, and that the reading was the last before a Fed board meeting.

Mint reported that the data reinforced bets that the Fed will raise rates by at least 25 basis points before the end of 2026. Inflation has stayed above the central bank's 2% target for around 5½ years, it said.
On the MCX, gold futures dropped ₹4,423, or 3.6%, to ₹1,17,906 per 10 grams, their lowest level in more than a year. Gold's losses in November have widened to ₹20,435.
Silver futures fell ₹8,800 per kg to ₹1,36,712, their lowest since September 2025. That followed a fall of ₹8,779 in the previous session and takes silver's losses in 2026 to nearly ₹1 lakh.

Mint said higher rate expectations make non-yielding assets such as gold and silver less attractive. A stronger dollar also makes dollar-priced commodities costlier for holders of other currencies. The dollar rebounded to 104 against a basket of currencies, supported also by a sell-off in global equities.

US stocks fell on Wednesday morning as investors weighed the inflation data and continued concern over the AI trade, The Guardian reported. The Nasdaq was down over 4%, the S&P 500 had lost over 2.5% and the Dow had dropped about 2%.

Several Fed officials have backed higher rates. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said last week that the Fed would need to raise rates again because inflation remained too high. Governor Christopher Waller indicated that a 50-basis-point increase could also be considered in December, Mint reported.

The US has also proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China, the European Union, Japan and India, according to Mint. They are meant to replace tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court. The Trump administration says they target what it describes as "overcapacity".

stories.headline: North Korea expels Swiss envoy, orders Pyongyang office closed
stories.dek: The Foreign Ministry cited Swiss sanctions on a children's camp that Bern accuses of taking part in the transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied areas.
stories.summary: North Korea declared the head of Switzerland's Pyongyang diplomatic office persona non grata and gave him 48 hours to leave, state media said on Wednesday. The office had reopened less than a month earlier.
body: North Korea on Wednesday declared the head of Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours, state media reported, less than a month after the office reopened.

The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Pak Hyon Su, director general of the Foreign Ministry's European Department, summoned the office head, Sylvain Astier, and handed him a memorandum demanding that the office be closed. PTI, citing KCNA, gave his name as Astier Sylvain.

Pyongyang said the step responded to Swiss sanctions on the Songdowon International Children's Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan, which it called an openly hostile act. "Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us," KCNA said.

Switzerland imposed the sanctions on November 4. Swiss authorities accused the camp of taking part in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea and of contributing to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children". The camp also hosts Chinese and Russian students, DW reported.

On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the sanctions. She said they infringed North Korea's sovereignty by denying it the ability to provide children with culture and recreation, and North Korea said it would consider closing the office.

Switzerland's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that the reopening was separate from its sanctions policy. "Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues," it said. Swiss authorities could not immediately be reached for comment on Wednesday.

Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in South Korea, told Reuters that North Korea was using Switzerland as a test case to show that sanctions and dialogue are incompatible. He said the move was a warning to the United States, which is seeking to reestablish contact. Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told AFP that Pyongyang, backed by China and Russia, wanted to make an example of Switzerland.

On Monday, Kim Jong Un received credentials from new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden. He said North Korea sought wider relations with countries that respect its sovereignty but would oppose attempts to restrict the rights and development of sovereign states.
keyFacts: North Korea gave the head of the Swiss office, Sylvain Astier, 48 hours to leave.
Switzerland sanctioned the Songdowon International Children's Camp in Wonsan on November 4.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis reopened the office in October, the first Swiss ministerial visit since 2003.

stories.background:
Switzerland has had diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and has long acted as an intermediary between Pyongyang and Western countries. Its office in Pyongyang closed in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The office operates under the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, which handles relations with North Korea. Pyongyang also has an embassy in Bern. Sweden, Poland and the Czech Republic are among the few European countries with missions in North Korea.
stories.whyItMatters: The expulsion removes Switzerland's recently restored diplomatic presence in North Korea, a country with few Western missions, and tests whether channels of dialogue can coexist with sanctions.

stories.headline: Ukraine says it hit two Samara refineries; Russia says retaliation is coming
stories.dek: Kyiv's foreign minister told Vladimir Putin to end the war if he wants the refinery attacks to stop, after the Russian president promised a response.
stories.summary: Ukraine said it struck two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, while local officials reported one death and power cuts. Putin pledged retaliation on Tuesday; Ukraine's foreign minister told him to stop complaining.
body: Ukraine said it struck two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight into Wednesday, while Russian officials reported one person killed in Samara and drone damage to industrial facilities in the city of Syzran.

Local authorities said on Wednesday, November 25, that industrial facilities in Syzran came under drone attack and that one person died in a drone strike on Samara, the regional capital. Syzran's mayor, Andrei Sovetkin, described the attack in a statement, and a video released with it showed smoke rising from a fire.

Syzran and Samara, both on the Volga River, host three major oil refineries. Unverified social media reports said at least two of them, the Syzran and Kuibyshev refineries, were hit. Reuters said it could not independently verify those reports.

Samara governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on social media that local air defence forces downed 145 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that the attack caused power outages. He asked residents not to share images of the aftermath. "Do not publish any photos or videos showing the aftermath of the attack," he wrote on VKontakte.
Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged retaliation for the Ukrainian strikes on Tuesday, November 24. According to CNBC, he called a response "inevitable".
Ukraine's foreign minister answered by telling Putin to "stop complaining", CNBC reported. He said Kyiv would stop attacking Russian refineries if Putin ended the war.

Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries eased somewhat after US President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire in mid-October, according to Reuters. They have picked up again sharply since the end of last month.

stories.headline: Supreme Court sets aside Vinay Kulkarni's suspended sentence, orders surrender
stories.dek: A bench of Justices PK Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar called the Karnataka High Court's July order 'perverse' and cancelled bail bonds of eight life convicts in the 2016 Yogesh Gowda murder.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside the Karnataka High Court order that had stayed former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni's conviction and suspended his life sentence. He and seven co-convicts must surrender within two weeks.
body: The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside a Karnataka High Court order that had stayed the conviction and suspended the life sentence of former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni in the 2016 murder of BJP leader Yogesh Gowda, and directed him to surrender within two weeks.

A bench of Justices PK Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar cancelled the bail bonds of Kulkarni and seven other life convicts. They must surrender before the concerned court. Hindustan Times reported that eight convicts are covered by the order; South First reported that 16 others were convicted along with Kulkarni.

The bench described the High Court's July 31 order as "perverse". It said the High Court had stayed the conviction on a "misconception" that Kulkarni would otherwise be disqualified as a member of the legislative assembly. "If that is how the power of the court to stay the judgment of conviction is to be interpreted then every convicted legislator would automatically become entitled to an order staying the conviction," the court said.

On suspension of sentence, the bench said: "It is a wrong notion that pendency of the criminal appeal and its remote possibility of hearing in near future can be a ground to suspend the sentence in grave offences like murder, dacoity, rape, ransom etc." It added that the matter concerned the equality and liberty of other convicts serving life terms.

The court noted that the High Court had not identified any "serious error" in the trial court's judgment that would make out a case for acquittal. It said a stay of conviction is an exceptional remedy requiring a "palpable mistake" in the verdict.

The Supreme Court was hearing appeals filed by the Karnataka government, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Gowda's family. The ruling does not dispose of the convicts' appeals against their convictions, which the High Court will continue to hear, South First reported. A copy of the order was awaited when that report was published.

A special court for MPs and MLAs convicted Kulkarni of murder and criminal conspiracy on April 15 and sentenced him to life imprisonment two days later. A Division Bench of the High Court, Justices Mohammed Nawaz and G Basavaraja, had on July 31 suspended his sentence and directed his release on bail pending the appeal.

Gowda, a Dharwad Zilla Panchayat member, was hacked to death at his gym in Saptapur, Dharwad, on June 15, 2016. The CBI described Kulkarni as the "mastermind" or "main conspirator". Kulkarni was disqualified as an MLA with effect from May 2.
The convicts have two weeks from Wednesday's order to surrender.
